cues.text: A Yes That Changed Everything

Little of Mary's early life is recorded in Scripture, though pious tradition, reaching back to the earliest centuries, holds that she was born to Sts. Joachim and Anne and raised in devout expectation of Israel's promised deliverance.
What Scripture does tell us, with unforgettable simplicity, is the moment that mattered above all others.
An angel appeared to a young girl in the obscure village of Nazareth , announcing that she would conceive and bear a son called the Son of the Most High.
Mary's response — may it be done to me according to your word — remains one of the most consequential sentences ever spoken by a human being.

Nothing compelled this yes; the invitation was offered, and freely, fully accepted, so that the Eternal Word could take flesh not by divine override but by the genuine consent of one small, faithful heart.
Full of Grace from the Beginning
The angel's greeting to Mary — hail, full of grace — became, over centuries of prayerful reflection, the seed of one of the Church's most cherished doctrines.
That doctrine holds that Mary, in view of her unique calling to be the Mother of God, was preserved from the stain of original sin from the very first moment of her own conception.
The Church calls this privilege the Immaculate Conception , formally defined as dogma by Pope Pius IX in 1854.
This was never taught as some special exemption earned by Mary's own merit.
Instead, it was a grace given entirely in view of her son's saving work, applied to her in advance.
This was the same redemption, Christ would win for all humanity on the cross, granted to his own mother at the very start of her life rather than only at its end.
Bearing God in the World
Mary's pregnancy carried her at once out of her own quiet concerns and into generous service of others: she traveled into the hill country to assist her elderly cousin Elizabeth .
Elizabeth was herself unexpectedly pregnant with the child who would become John the Baptist .
There, Mary sang the great hymn of praise the Church still prays every evening, the Magnificat , proclaiming a God who lifts up the lowly and fills the hungry with good things.
She gave birth to her son in the poverty of a stable in Bethlehem and presented him in the Temple according to the Law.
She fled with him into Egypt to escape a jealous king's murderous decree.

When he was twelve, she searched for him in anguish for three days after he remained behind in Jerusalem—a mother's ordinary joys and terrors, lived out around the extraordinary reality of the child she carried.
Present at the Wedding, Present at the Cross
The Gospel of John shows us Mary at a wedding in Cana, noticing quietly that the wine had run out.
She brings the need to her son with a simple, trusting word — they have no wine .
This small scene has long been read as an image of her continuing intercession on behalf of ordinary human need.
It is also read as an image of Christ's willingness to act at his mother's gentle prompting even before, in his own words, his hour had come.
The same Gospel shows her standing at the foot of the cross when nearly every other follower had scattered in fear.
There, she watched her son die the death of a criminal and received from his own lips, even in his final agony, a new son to care for in the beloved disciple.
In that one figure standing beside her was gathered, symbolically, the whole Church.
A Heart Pierced, and a Faith That Held
The elderly Simeon had warned Mary, when she presented her infant son in the Temple, that a sword would pierce her own soul as well.
That prophecy was fulfilled most fully at Calvary, where she watched her child suffer and die without any miraculous intervention a mother's heart might have begged for.
And yet nothing in the Gospel accounts suggests her faith wavered even at this darkest hour.
Rather, she stood — the Gospel's own verb, so simple and so strong — present, attentive, and unbroken in trust.
She was a model for every believer of what it looks like to hold fast to faith precisely when consolation is entirely withdrawn.
Present at Pentecost, and Assumed into Glory
After the Resurrection, Mary appears one final time in the New Testament narrative, gathered with the Apostles in the upper room.
They await in prayerful expectation of the Holy Spirit's coming at Pentecost —present, once again, at the very birth of the Church, as she had once been present at the birth of her son.

Scripture is silent about the end of Mary's earthly life, but the Church's ancient and constant tradition holds that Mary, having completed her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory .
Formally defined as dogma by Pope Pius XII in 1950, this was, the Church has always believed, a fitting completion for the one who carried the Author of Life in her own body.
It was also a promise, held out to every believer, of what awaits all who are united to her son.
Legacy
The Church's devotion to Mary, expressed across two thousand years in art, prayer, doctrine, and pilgrimage beyond counting, flows entirely from her unique relationship to her son.
She is honored not as a rival to Christ's mediation but as the one who, by her free and total consent, freely cooperated in God's plan for the Incarnation.
She continues, the Church believes, to intercede for her children with a mother's unwavering tenderness.
In her simple yes at Nazareth, every believer finds an image of what an entire human life surrendered to the will of God can become.
